subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Rubber Hand Illusion
description: One-minute skill: The Rubber Hand Illusion.

hook.text: Put a rubber hand on the table, hide your real hand, and stroke both in sync. Soon the rubber hand feels like yours.

buildup.text: Botvinick and Cohen showed this in 1998. Within minutes, people flinch when the rubber hand is threatened.

discovery.text: The brain integrates visual and tactile signals to build body ownership. When they align, it claims the fake hand.

twist.text: Temperature in the real hand drops during the illusion. The brain literally withdraws resources from the disowned limb.

climax.text: This illusion inspired prosthetic design: if the brain can adopt a rubber hand, it might adopt an artificial one.

punchline.text: Your brain decides what's 'your body' based on sensory votes.

quiz.question: What causes the rubber hand illusion?
options: Integration of matching visual and tactile signals

details.summary: In the rubber hand illusion, synchronized stroking of a hidden real hand and a visible rubber hand causes people to feel the rubber hand as their own. This reveals that body ownership is not fixed but is actively constructed from multisensory evidence that the brain integrates in real time.
details.whyItMatters: The rubber hand illusion proves that body ownership is a perceptual construction, not an innate given. This has major implications for prosthetics and virtual reality.
takeaways: Synchronized touch can make you feel a fake hand as yours
Body ownership is constructed from vision, touch, and position
The illusion reveals body representation is flexible and updatable

faq.question: What happens in the brain during the rubber hand illusion?
faq.answer: Brain imaging shows changes in premotor cortex and intraparietal areas associated with body representation. The brain updates its body map to include the rubber hand. Physiological responses follow: threatening the rubber hand produces real fear.

faq.question: How does this apply to prosthetic limbs?
faq.answer: If the brain can adopt a rubber hand through synchronized touch, it can potentially adopt prosthetic limbs too. Researchers are developing prosthetics with sensory feedback that trigger the same ownership mechanisms. This could make artificial limbs feel like genuine body parts rather than tools.
